title: Choosing Flow or Apex for a business operation
summary: Choose an implementation from the shape of the work, its transaction boundaries, and the team's ability to maintain it.
prerequisites: Junior record-triggered Flow and bulk-safe Apex.
learningObjectives: Implement a small operation without duplicating responsibility.

sections.heading: Understand the mechanism
body: Northstar wants an automatic follow-up when Irina's test drive is confirmed. A Flow can be a clear choice when the rule is straightforward, administrators maintain it, and existing automation remains understandable. A more complex allocation algorithm or a highly reused typed service may fit Apex better. Neither the number of clicks nor a developer's preferred tool is a sufficient decision rule.

Start with the business operation, not the technology. State what triggers it, which records it reads and writes, the expected batch size, who maintains it, and what should happen when one record fails. Then locate the transaction boundary: must the follow-up succeed together with the confirmation, or may it be processed later? Moving work asynchronously changes the product's failure behavior, even if it reduces synchronous work.

Flow and Apex can coexist, but ownership of a rule must remain clear. If a Flow and trigger both create the same reminder, each may be individually correct while the combined application duplicates work. Use one orchestrator for the operation and call a reusable service only where that separation has value. A diagram showing two independent owners is a warning to resolve before implementation.

A decision should include the surrounding org. One more simple Flow in an already dense automation landscape may increase diagnostic difficulty. Conversely, a large framework for a three-condition rule can burden the next maintainer. Evaluate observability, testability, access enforcement, expected volume, and the likely next requirement. Record the tradeoff so future developers can reconsider it when the conditions change.

callouts.text: Choose the smallest understandable implementation that meets the actual transaction, volume, and maintenance requirements.

sections.heading: Northstar Motors worked example
body: Compare three requests. First, set a field on the same appointment when it changes to Confirmed. Second, create one follow-up record after confirmation, with a defined retry policy. Third, allocate vehicles across hundreds of appointments using a conflict-resolution algorithm. These differ in data access, failure handling, and complexity; they should not receive the same answer merely because all begin with a record change.

For the hands-on part, use a simple same-record rule: when a Test Drive first becomes Confirmed, reject confirmation without Vehicle__c, Customer__c, or Scheduled_At__c. No new fields are required. A validation rule is worth considering before either Flow or Apex because the requirement is to prevent invalid data. Comparing three tools is useful when the third is the simplest expression of the requirement.

callouts.text: Have you distinguished preventing invalid data from performing a follow-up action?

sections.heading: Build and inspect
body: Use existing starter fields and a separate training branch. Inventory active validation, Flow, and triggers on Test_Drive__c before adding another implementation.

steps.title: Write the decision table
steps.instruction: For each request, list trigger, inputs, writes, volume, error policy, maintenance owner, and transaction needs. Include validation rules as a candidate where appropriate.
steps.expected: The choice follows constraints instead of tool loyalty.

steps.title: Implement one responsibility
steps.instruction: Implement the required-field confirmation rule using the selected mechanism. Disable competing experimental implementations in the training org.
steps.expected: Exactly one rule owns the validation behavior.

steps.title: Verify boundaries
steps.instruction: Try valid and invalid confirmations, a later harmless edit, and a 200-record operation. Capture which records fail and why.
steps.expected: The observed failure policy matches the decision document.

sections.heading: Failure cases and boundaries
body: A Flow is not automatically safe merely because its designer is visual. Queries and writes inside repeated paths still need volume analysis. Apex is not automatically maintainable merely because it is covered by tests.
A successful single-record UI save does not establish behavior for a bulk integration. The same requirement should be checked through the operation that will actually use it.

callouts.text: Do not implement the same business rule independently in Flow and Apex without a deliberate ownership boundary.

exercise.title: Defend an implementation choice
exercise.brief: Choose and implement the confirmation rule, then explain how two larger variants would change your decision.
steps: Compare at least two candidates and the transaction requirements.
Test valid, invalid, repeat-edit, and bulk cases.
acceptance: The choice mentions maintenance and volume.
No duplicate automation performs the same responsibility.
The failure policy is demonstrated rather than implied.
exercise.stretch: Explain one limitation and propose a small follow-up experiment before extending the implementation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Is Flow always preferable for a simple UI?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. The relevant complexity lies in the business operation and existing automation, not just the screen.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why consider validation rules?
knowledgeCheck.answer: They directly express an invariant that must block invalid saves without creating another orchestration layer.

knowledgeCheck.question: What changes when work moves async?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The original save and later result are no longer one atomic user operation; status, errors, and retries become visible concerns.

recap: Start with requirements and transaction boundaries.
Reconsider the tool when constraints change.
